newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parliament set to outlaw rape in marriage.
newsitem.headline: German parliament set to outlaw rape in marriage.

text.p: The Bonn parliament on Thursday debated a cross-party bill to make rape within marriage a criminal offence, bringing Germany into line with most of its European Union partners after a quarter of a century of wrangling,
The German statute book has until now defined rape as extra-marital, meaning that a husband who raped his wife could be convicted only if he used violence to inflict bodily harm.

The new bill is the fifth one launched since 1972. As a cross-party motion, it will go to a free vote without party constraint, and so has more chance than its predecessors of overcoming long-standing conservative opposition to become law.
It sets a 15-year maximum penalty, and widens the definition of rape to include sexual abuse apart from penetration.

The bill also for the first time uses gender-neutral language to make rape of a man by either sex punishable, and it accepts that someone can be forced into sex with emotional rather than physical violence.
"Marriage is not a legal vacuum," Women's Affairs Minister Claudia Nolte told parliament before it voted to send the bill on to the committee stage.
"If a violent husband destroys the trust that a marriage is built on, he does not deserve to be protected but must be punished...Let us finally make rape within marriage a crime."

There has been broad agreement for several years on the need to recognise the crime, and the lower house even approved the measure a year ago. But wrangling about a whether a wife should have the right to withdraw her complaint meant it failed to become law.
Nolte swallowed her own belief that this right should be maintained, and urged deputies not to let squabbles over a secondary issue block consensus on the cross-party draft.
The idea that, by marrying, a woman automatically consents to sex on demand with her husband was banished from the statute books of most Western European countries in the 1980s or early 1990s.

In a survey in Germany by Nolte's ministry, one-seventh of women between 20 and 59 said they had been subjected at least once to rape or sexual coercion, three-quarters of them at the hands of a husband or partner.
Women in Germany are more likely to suffer sexual violence than any other kind of violent attack, robbery or burglary.

Most of the previous bills succumbed to conservative opposition led by the Christian Social Union, Chancellor Kohl's junior coalition partners from mostly-Catholic Bavaria, who saw the idea of marital rape as a feminist myth and a threat to family life.

The new bill, which has enough cross-party support to pass easily through the Upper House and subsequent readings, picks up the demand of the centre-left opposition that a woman should not be allowed to withdraw a criminal complaint against her husband.
They argued that a wife was acutely vulnerable to pressure from her husband, and that protection from this pressure should take precedence over the need to allow for a reconciliation.
